claims.claim: The Sun accounts for about 99.8 percent of the mass of the solar system.
The Sun is about 93 million miles (150 million kilometers) from Earth, a distance astronomers call one astronomical unit (AU).

The photosphere, the Sun's visible surface, has a temperature of about 5,500 C (NASA gives 10,000 F; OpenStax gives about 5,800 K), while the core reaches about 15 million C (NASA gives 27 million F).

The Sun's interior is layered: a core where fusion occurs, a radiative zone where energy travels outward as repeatedly absorbed and re-emitted photons, and an outer convective zone where hot plasma rises and sinks; the visible surface is the photosphere, above which lie the chromosphere and the corona.

The Sun's energy comes from nuclear fusion: deep in the core, four hydrogen nuclei fuse to form one helium nucleus, and the small loss of mass is converted into energy; nearly all of the energy is produced within about 150,000 kilometers of the center.
The corona, the Sun's outer atmosphere, is much hotter than the photosphere (up to about 2 million C) even though it is farther from the core, and it gradually becomes the solar wind.

Sunspots are cooler regions of the photosphere (about 3,800 K at their centers versus about 5,800 K for the photosphere) that appear dark only in contrast with their surroundings, and their numbers rise and fall in a cycle averaging about 11 years.

Solar flares are sudden eruptions that release bursts of radiation including X-rays and ultraviolet; coronal mass ejections are bubbles of plasma, mainly protons and electrons, ejected into space at hundreds of kilometers per second (about 500-1000 km/s).

When solar wind or coronal mass ejection material reaches Earth, it can brighten auroras, drag satellites through a heated and expanded upper atmosphere, induce power-grid surges (as in the March 1989 storm that left parts of Quebec without power for hours), degrade GPS signals, and increase radiation exposure for astronauts - effects studied as space weather.

The Sun is an ordinary star: NASA describes it as average in size, notes that stars up to 100 times larger have been found, and states that billions of stars like the Sun are scattered across the Milky Way galaxy.
Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to travel from the Sun to Earth: 150,000,000 km divided by 300,000 km/s is about 500 seconds (arithmetic from the sourced distance).

conflictingEvidence.issue: The photosphere temperature is quoted as 10,000 F (5,500 C) by NASA and about 5,800 K by OpenStax.
positions: NASA Sun Facts: 'a relatively cool 10,000 F (5,500 C)' for the photosphere.
OpenStax Astronomy 2e: effective temperature 5,800 K (Table 15.1) and photosphere temperature about 5,800 K (Figure 15.5 caption).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The figures agree within rounding: 10,000 F converts to about 5,540 C and 5,800 K to about 5,530 C. The lesson states 'about 5,500 C' and cites both sources.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The Earth-Sun distance is given as 93 million miles (150 million km) by NASA and as 1 AU = 149,597,892 km by OpenStax.
positions: NASA Sun Facts: 'about 93 million miles (150 million kilometers) from Earth'.
OpenStax Astronomy 2e Table 15.1: mean distance 1 AU (149,597,892 km).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both describe the same mean Earth-Sun distance, one AU. The lesson uses 'about 93 million miles (150 million kilometers), a distance astronomers call one astronomical unit (AU)' and cites both sources.

sourceRecords.title: 16.2 Mass, Energy, and the Theory of Relativity, Astronomy 2e
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl (server-rendered HTML). Supports the fusion mechanism: a three-step process fuses four hydrogen nuclei into one helium nucleus, the product is slightly less massive, and the lost mass is converted into energy; fusion requires temperatures above about 12 million K and nearly all of the Sun's energy is produced within about 150,000 km of the center; photons from core reactions take roughly 100,000 to 1,000,000 years to reach the surface. Used for original synthesis only.
